full_text:
The king lifted the Vetala again. The Vetala resumed:

"In Ujjayini's bustling bazaar, a humble village boy brought a shiny yellow metal ring to an expert goldsmith, Swarnakar. The boy said: 'My grandfather found this in the field. I know nothing of metals; is it worth a copper coin to buy bread?'

The goldsmith tested the metal and realized instantly it was rare, pure, ancient gold worth fifty gold dinars. Hiding his excitement, Swarnakar sneered: 'It is mere cheap brass. Out of charity, I will give you two copper coins.' The boy happily took the coins and departed.

Later that evening, Swarnakar rushed to sell the ring to a foreign merchant for seventy dinars. But upon deeper chemical inspection, the foreign merchant discovered the outer layer was thin gilt over iron slag—a clever fake made decades earlier! Swarnakar had spent his day cheating a boy, only to discover his prize was worthless slag.

Tell me, Vikram: did the boy deceive the goldsmith, or did the goldsmith deceive himself?"

King Vikramaditya answered: "The goldsmith deceived himself. The boy came with honest ignorance and asked only for bread. The goldsmith acted with deliberate deceit, intending to defraud the boy. His own greed blinded him to proper testing. Greed is a mirror that reflects the fraud of the schemer back upon his own head."

"True wisdom, O King!" chuckled the Vetala, and flew away.
moral: Greed blinds the seeker; taking advantage of another's presumed ignorance often exposes one's own folly.
